segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Phoebe Langton came down the staircase of Amberlight House first, and found Mrs Pike in the hall with one hand already on the newel post.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: My dear. The door was standing open to the lane. Where is the chain?

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: There is no chain, ma'am. There is a trunk with a handle come away, and a young lady who fainted picking up her letters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Harker had come down behind her. He stopped three steps up and spoke over Phoebe's head to both women.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: Miss Fairfax was to have been married in June. Her intended's mother said, before nine people, that she had gone after a dead man's money. It was broken off in April, and she came here where no one knew her face.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: You may carry that down the lane with my name at the end of it. A grief the parish knows is easier for her to walk through than a madness it has guessed at.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: That is a wicked thing for a mother to say.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: It is, and I never once said madness. Grief, I said. A sorrow is quite another article.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Hale pushed her spectacles up into her hair and said nothing. Mrs Pike was looking from Harker on the stair to Phoebe at the foot of it.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: This gentleman settled your account at the draper's and would not put his name to it. That is not meanness, my dear. I shall expect to hear something by Lady Day.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: I shall repeat it exactly as I had it, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: Then repeat the one pound eleven with it, and say it was owed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Monday morning Augusta Fairfax crossed the yard in black bombazine, cut to her own measure, taken standing up on the Saturday. Mr Rowe held the schoolroom door for her.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: I should like to hear the youngest read, if you will have me. I am not fit for much else yet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Ludd boy had put his ear to that wall and heard her crying through it. He read her four lines about a ship and got two of them right.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At dusk Phoebe walked down the lane with Harker beside her, because he had said he would see her to the green and she had not troubled to argue it.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: I gave you a poplin gown worn through at the elbow and told you to manage. It is still on the chair in my hall. I have not been able to put it anywhere.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: And I stood in the lane counting three guineas into my palm and thought the worst of you. We were both wrong in the same hall, sir, within five minutes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the turn she looked back. The shutters were off the main block. There was a candle in every window of it. The east wing was lit too, where Mr Rowe was locking up.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: Send your bill to the house for Miss Fairfax's mourning. Put your name to it, and I shall put mine under it.
